output.headline: Patrick Stewart, who brought gravitas to both Shakespeare and sci-fi, dies at 86
output.bodyHtml:
Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British stage and screen actor celebrated in equal measure for Shakespeare and science fiction, has died at 86, closing a career that ran from the Royal Shakespeare Company to the bridge of the Starship Enterprise and the X-Men's Professor Charles Xavier.

Stewart died on Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’, said Kelly Bush Novak, his longtime spokesperson, to the Hollywood Reporter.

Related: Patrick Stewart – a life in pictures

‘He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,’ she wrote. ‘We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.’

With his authoritative baritone voice and commanding visage, Stewart was already a staple of the British stage by the late 1980s when, at 47, he was cast as a greying Capt Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: the Next Generation, the first live-action spin-off of the groundbreaking 1960s TV series. Over seven seasons onboard the Starship Enterprise, Stewart’s even-keeled performance and steely directives – ‘engage!’ and ‘make it so’ – turned him into a global star.

Stewart reprised his role in four feature film spin-offs – Star Trek Generations (1994), Star Trek: First Contact (1996), Star Trek: Insurrection (1998) and Star Trek: Nemesis (2002) – as well as the TV series Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 until 2023.

His longtime friend, fellow Shakespearean actor and X-Men co-star Ian McKellen called him ‘the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic’.

‘Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end,’ he wrote on social media. ‘You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.’

Harriet Walter, who knew Stewart for more than 40 years and acted opposite him on stage in Antony and Cleopatra at the RSC in 2006, told BBC Newsnight that the world is ‘going to be very poor’ without him.

‘I can’t really imagine a world without him,’ she said. ‘It’s like a huge giant tree has fallen in the forest. I’ve never heard a bad word against him.’

Fellow Star Trek actor William Shatner paid tribute on social media. ‘From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did,’ he wrote. ‘Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.’

Related: ‘On stage, I could escape’: Sir Patrick Stewart on childhood trauma and acting success

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original series, also wrote about Stewart on Bluesky. ‘He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity,’ he posted. ‘Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.’

His other most well-known role was playing Prof Charles Xavier in the X-Men series. The actor had found work hard to obtain after feeling typecast as a result of his Star Trek role but had been intrigued by working with director Bryan Singer for 2000’s X-Men.

He went on to play the role in seven films and will be seen reprising the role in this December’s Avengers: Doomsday.

His X-Men co-star Hugh Jackman shared on Instagram: ‘We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.’

Marvel chief Kevin Feige has paid tribute in a statement calling him ‘brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas … Away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor. It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.’

Stewart’s other film roles included the gay comedy Jeffrey, romantic thriller Conspiracy Theory, violent horror Green Room and voice roles in Ted, Gnomeo & Juliet and, most recently, The Sheep Detectives.

Born on 13 July 1940 in the small industrial village of Mirfield, England, Stewart was the youngest of three sons born to Alfred Stewart, a British military veteran turned semi-skilled labourer, and Gladys Stewart, a weaver at a textile factory. His childhood, in a small house with no running hot water, was marred by alcoholism and domestic violence, a situation he later described, in an article for the Guardian from 2009, as ‘barely tolerable’.

He found respite in acting, first in school – he was 12 when an English teacher assigned him the part of Shylock in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice – and then local drama groups. ‘I managed to find my own refuge in acting,’ he wrote. ‘The stage was a far safer place for me than anything I had to live through at home – it offered escape. I could be someone else, in another place, in another time.’

After graduating from secondary school at 15, he worked as a local reporter and furniture salesman before a local arts council provided the funding to attend the prestigious Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, where he enrolled in 1957, at 17. Having shed his Yorkshire accent, he took his first professional theatre role two years later, and in 1966 joined the Royal Shakespeare Company. During his 16 years with the company, Stewart developed a reputation as one of the finest thespians of his era and a representative of Shakespeare to new audiences; it was while conducting master classes on Shakespeare in LA, at the invitation of a friend, that he first caught the eye of a TV casting director for Star Trek.

Stewart made his Broadway debut in 1971 in Peter Brook’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, and appeared again 20 years later in a solo production of A Christmas Carol. The holiday season show, which he revived in 1992, 1994 and 2001, received a Drama Desk award.

Over the course of his career, Stewart embodied many of Shakespeare’s signature roles, including Macbeth, Othello, Prospero, Shylock and Mark Antony. He was the recipient of two Laurence Olivier awards – in 1979, for Antony and Cleopatra, and in 2009 for Hamlet – as well as a Grammy in 1996 for a spoken word children’s album Prokofiev: Peter and the Wolf. He was also nominated for a Tony and four Emmys.

His final major stage role was in 2016, when he appeared as Hirst in Harold Pinter’s No Man’s Land at London’s Wyndham Theatre. In 2023, he released his memoir called Making It So.

Stewart was a vocal fan of Huddersfield Town FC since he was a child and was seen cheering them on most recently in 2024. In a Facebook post from the official team, he was called ‘a titan of his craft and a legend and hero to millions worldwide’.

Stewart was married three times: to theater choreographer Sheila Falconer, from 1966 until 1990 and with whom he had two children, fellow actors Daniel and Sophie; to Star Trek producer Wendy Neuss from 2000 until 2003; and to jazz musician Sunny Ozell from 2013 until his death. His friend and occasional collaborator Ian McKellen, with whom Stewart starred in two Broadway productions in 2013, officiated his final wedding after a rehearsal.

‘I think I’ve been in denial about my life for a very long time,’ he said to the Guardian in a 2023 interview. ‘I never really took on board how successful I had become. Even today I sometimes think, “You’re a lucky son of a bitch, Patrick,” when something unexpected or good happens to me.’
output.standfirst: The Star Trek and X-Men actor, celebrated equally for his Shakespearean stage work, died at 86 at his Los Angeles home, after ‘a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia’.

output.headline: Healey points to Milburn and Timms reviews on welfare reform
output.bodyHtml:
John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, pointing instead to reviews of how the benefits system works, even as warnings mount that his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.

Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking big tax and spending decisions.

In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030.

Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to ‘a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments’ – including real-term budget cuts.

‘Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,’ she said, adding that meant Healey could face ‘another season of damaging speculation about tax rises’.

To underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: ‘We have to bring the benefits bill down.’ The welfare bill itself will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets.

Asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election, Healey had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament. ‘There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,’ he said. ‘We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.’

Related: Budget 2026: what it means for your wallet, your mortgage and your pay

However, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: ‘It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.’

Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms on disability benefits.

Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment.

The Office for Budget Responsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.

With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars.

But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view than the prime minister on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: ‘Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.’

Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: ‘I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.’

The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a ‘scattergun’ approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package.

The Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week.

Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: ‘Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.

‘Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.’

Related: John Healey faces questions over budget leak that moved bank share prices

Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further.

The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: ‘It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.’

As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs.

The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn.

Miller said that was a ‘reasonable’ decision to make, but ‘a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news’.
output.standfirst: The chancellor says there is no timetable for welfare cuts this parliament, pointing instead to reviews on youth employment and disability support, as experts say his ‘scattergun’ budget leaves a £28bn shortfall.
output.progress: Healey points to forthcoming reviews by Alan Milburn on youth employment and Stephen Timms on disability benefits to bring down welfare costs.

output.headline: Israeli officials and president reject Netanyahu's baseless vote-buying claims
output.bodyHtml:
Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after his claim that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to ‘steal’ Tuesday’s election – in which his coalition lost its parliamentary majority – was quickly rejected by Israeli officials.

Police officers, members of the election committee and a range of other government officials quickly disowned the prime minister’s allegations. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for ‘tarnishing an entire community’.

Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel, supposedly funded by foreign money.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.

‘It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,’ Eisenkot said in a video message.

On Wednesday night, the prime minister posted a statement by Likud online, which described the claimed violations as ‘an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule’.

Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, holding the balance of power.

Final results released early on Friday local time showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset and Eisenkot’s bloc taking 48 seats. Joint List and Ra’am won the remaining 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.

The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition from voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.

The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: ‘It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.’

Opposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.

Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. ‘Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,’ Jabareen said, adding that he ‘refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided’.

Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted ‘without fear or favour,’ and with ‘the utmost caution’, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.

The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.

The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to ‘avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy’.

It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government ‘categorically’ denied any involvement in the elections.

The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.

On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.

Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.

Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.

The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist ‘Change’ bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.

One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.

Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.

‘This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,’ Tibi told the Reuters news agency.

Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the ‘Change’ bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are being accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.

‘This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,’ Bennett wrote on X.
output.standfirst: Israel’s police, election officials and president have all pushed back against Benjamin Netanyahu’s claim that Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal Tuesday’s election, in which his coalition lost its majority.
output.progress: Israel’s election committee and police say the vote-buying claims are groundless, while the president has rebuked Netanyahu for ‘tarnishing an entire community’.

output.headline: Colleague steps in as MP takes complaint over Farage encounter to parliament
output.bodyHtml:
A male Liberal Democrat colleague stepped in after Nigel Farage grabbed and pushed aside a female MP at the state opening of parliament, Caroline Voaden has said.

Voaden gave her account of the incident, which took place in May, after Farage revealed on Wednesday that there had been a “physical altercation” in parliament that led him to avoid the budget.

Voaden told the Guardian: “He was trying to get out of the chamber and instead of just asking if he could go past, he said: ‘Let me past’. I turned round and said: ‘No, you can wait your turn like everyone else’. He grabbed me by the arm or the shoulder, pushed me to one side and tried to push past me. One of my colleagues tried to stop him because he thought I was going to fall down the stairs. And then we all shuffled down.

“Quite deliberately, he grabbed me by the arm from behind and pushed me to one side so that I fell into a colleague or the wall on the other side. I was really taken aback and really angry because I think you just don’t behave like that in any workplace, let alone the chamber of the House of Commons. It was rude. It was nasty.”

The male Lib Dem MP who stepped in is understood to be Max Wilkinson, with sources saying he put a hand on Farage’s shoulder, “fairly gently” grabbed him and told him he could not do that to another MP.

Voaden said she had complained to the serjeant at arms, who she believed had written to Farage asking him to apologise, and had also raised the incident with the speaker. “Nothing ever came of it,” she said.

A Reform UK source disputed her account, saying it was “not true at all, it was the Lib Dem MPs being aggressive towards Nigel. This is typical Lib Dem dishonesty in an attempt to stay relevant.”

Reform sources also suggested a video from the Commons showed her account was wrong, but the Lib Dems said the incident took place before the footage started.

The row erupted after the Reform leader said he had skipped John Healey’s budget speech in the Commons on Wednesday because his seat reservation had been moved and he decided to give it a “wide berth” in order to “avoid conflict” in the chamber.

He claimed he had been involved in a “physical altercation” with another MP on the day of the state opening of parliament in May.

It later emerged that his reservation had been removed by Commons staff because it did not have the proper date stamp.

Related: Nigel Farage skips budget in Commons over seating ‘altercation’ concerns

Daisy Cooper, the Lib Dem deputy leader, told Sky News on Thursday morning that her party’s MPs were involved in the May incident mentioned by Farage.

She said: “My understanding – I didn’t see it, I wasn’t there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that.

“I didn’t see it, I didn’t witness what happened, but that was several months ago.

“And let’s be really clear: it’s Reform UK that had a problem at their conference with bundling female journalists and members out of their hall. So, we’ll take no lessons from them on this.”

Afterwards, Voaden posted on social media in response to Farage’s claim that he was at risk of “another physical altercation”: “We both know that’s not true Nigel don’t we?

“I’m still waiting for the apology you were required to write to me … Though I won’t hold my breath.”

Asked for a response to the accusations, Robert Jenrick, Reform’s shadow chancellor, said: “You know what? I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates.

“The thing about Reform politicians is, yeah, we love parliament, the institution of parliament. I go there every day. I speak in parliament. I represent my constituents.

“But I’m much more interested about, actually, the issues, trying to change this country, getting out and about outside of the bubble. And I’m not interested in even responding, dignifying the nonsense that Daisy Cooper is talking about there.”
output.standfirst: Caroline Voaden's colleague intervened after she says Nigel Farage grabbed her arm and pushed her aside at the state opening of parliament in May; her complaint to Commons authorities has so far brought no apology.
output.progress: Voaden said she complained to the serjeant at arms, who she believed had asked Farage to apologise, and separately raised it with the speaker.

output.headline: Met refers itself to watchdog, alerts FBI and Philippine police over Meghan letter
output.bodyHtml:
The Metropolitan police has referred itself to the police watchdog over potential errors in its handling of a 2019 letter that flagged dangers to the security of the Duchess of Sussex posed by her father.

The Guardian understands the Met is now sending details of the letter to the FBI in the US and law enforcement in the Philippines, where Markle lived until May, as well as Thai counterparts.

The key problem for the Met is its admission that it did not share the letter with law enforcement agencies overseas, and that issue has been referred to the police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

Met Commander Adam Slonecki, who leads its Protection Command, said the letter had been sent in 2019 to the Fixated Threats Assessment Centre: “The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.

“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.”

Slonecki added: “A voluntary referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.”

An IOPC spokesperson said: “We have received a voluntary conduct referral from the Met police, which relates to the handling of a letter it received in 2019 involving allegations of offending. We are now assessing the referral before deciding what further action may be required.”

Possible options include the police watchdog independently investigating or sending the matter back for the Met to investigate.

The Met cannot find a copy of the 2019 warning letter in its systems, and asked the Duchess of Sussex to send the copy she had to assist Britain’s biggest force to better understand its decision making seven years ago, which she did.

The allegations about the letter and alleged Met failings surfaced publicly a week ago. The Met has been unable to find its own copy of the letter making the claims, alleged to have been written by Markle’s former wife.

The letter made allegations about Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, who is facing claims of child sexual abuse images offending linked to the Philippines, which he denies.

It was allegedly written by his former wife and the Met says the letter was passed seven years ago to the private office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, who were then both working royals.

The Guardian understands that the long letter made claims about Markle’s activities in the US, the Philippines and Thailand.

The Met said it did not investigate as the allegations related to potential unlawful activity overseas.

Markle, now in the US, has admitted paying for sex but denies possessing material that would be illegal.

On Saturday Jonvic Remulla, the Philippine interior minister, told the Guardian that all signs point to Markle being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” and that a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”.

Officials and investigators in the Philippines are examining digital images alleged to belong to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, and alleged to have been found at his former home in the south-east Asian country.

Meghan’s half-brother, also called Thomas, reported to Philippine authorities last week the alleged discovery of child sexual abuse images.

The scale of embarrassment for the Met will depend on whether investigators in the Philippines assess that the allegations relating to child sexual abuse images have any credence.
output.standfirst: The Met referred itself to the watchdog and is alerting overseas police to a 2019 letter it failed to share for seven years, amid child sexual abuse allegations against Meghan's father, which he denies.
output.progress: The Met is alerting the FBI and police in the Philippines and Thailand, while the watchdog assesses its self-referral.

output.headline: Experts make the case for treating online misogyny as a public health issue
output.bodyHtml:
The manosphere and online misogyny should be treated by the government as a public health issue, in the same way as obesity or smoking, experts have said.

Writing in the Lancet, the authors of a new report argue that a coordinated response is needed, involving governments, schools, health services and community organisations, similar to the public-health response to tobacco use and ultra-processed food.

Prof Kent Buse, a co-author of the paper and co-founder of the social justice thinktank Global 50/50, said: “This is a business model, not a fringe. Outrage and grievance are good for business, so the system rewards the most extreme content. Expect the playbook that served tobacco so well: blame the individual, and call regulation an attack on freedom. Public health has a tested toolkit for commercial harms and we should use it.”

He added: “Boys and men are not the problem. The problem is the conditions that leave them isolated and without a secure future, and the companies that profit from their anger and insecurity.”

Prof Sarah Hawkes, the report’s other author, said: “The manosphere offers boys and young men belonging, identity and an explanation for why life feels hard.

“Those needs are real. A response that only removes the manosphere, without offering something credible in its place, will fail. We need to offer boys something better, not just tell them what to avoid.”

Mark Brooks, the policy and communications director at the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys, welcomed the report’s position that it was a public health issue and that men, boys, women and girls were all victims of this content.

“Far too often, the manosphere discussion has positioned all men and boys as a problem and not taken into account the broader economic, educational and cultural challenges that drive their engagement,” he said.

“Not all men and boys engage with this content equally. We are currently working on research to identify who is most at risk.”

“Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions, and masculine identity is commodified through products and paid content that normalise and reinforce health-harming and performance-oriented masculinities,” the authors write.

The report defines the manosphere as “a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny and male victimisation”.

It goes on to outline how the manosphere has evolved into a highly lucrative online industry that makes money by promoting “the most extreme expressions of misogyny and aggrieved masculinity”.

Related: UK government to give £15m to anti-misogyny fund amid ‘manosphere’ concerns

The authors also point to growing disengagement from education among boys around the world, as well as loneliness, money worries and social exclusion, which can leave young men searching for a sense of belonging. These problems, they say, can make them more vulnerable to online communities that offer simple explanations for their difficulties and often encourage them to blame women and feminism.
output.standfirst: A new Lancet report urges a coordinated, tobacco-style public health response to the manosphere, a lucrative industry profiting from extreme misogyny to which isolated, disengaged young men are vulnerable.
output.progress: Lancet authors Kent Buse and Sarah Hawkes call for a coordinated public health response from schools, health services and governments.

output.headline: Xi Jinping says corruption fight goes on, as scepticism over motive grows
output.bodyHtml:
China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.

A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.

Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022 – meaning more than 25 per cent of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.

Related: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders

Among those confirmed as expelled were Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang; other absences went unexplained.

Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said in a post on X: “More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline.”

Party governance was this week’s theme. Since taking power in 2012, Xi has pursued a campaign against corruption in the party’s ranks, which in recent years has intensified to take in officials at the highest levels of the party and the military – raising questions over whether the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.

Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey.”

A series of purges has reduced the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army, to just two members: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.

Zhang was promoted to the politburo, the CCP’s highest ruling body, this week, making him the only military member of the senior leadership body.

The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event that happens every five years and is expected to be held next in the second half of 2027, when Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party – making him the longest-ruling leader of Communist China since Mao Zedong.

The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo are due to be refreshed at next year’s congress, though many analysts believe the recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are now few suitable candidates for promotion.

output.headline: Permanent early-release scheme under Sentencing Act replaces emergency measure
output.bodyHtml:
A permanent early-release scheme came into force on 1 October under the Sentencing Act 2026, replacing the emergency measures that had freed tens of thousands of prisoners early as ministers sought to ease overcrowding – even as new figures show more people were recalled to jail in England and Wales in the first half of this year than were released.

Despite those efforts, more people were recalled to jails in England and Wales in the first half of this year than were released, according to the Ministry of Justice figures published on Thursday.

MoJ data shows 12,338 people were recalled to custody between the start of April and the end of June, against 12,278 who were released – continuing a trend set between January and March, when 13,193 people were returned to prison and 12,977 released.

A total of 52,716 prisoners were put back behind bars in the year to June after breaching the terms of their licence – a rise of 27 per cent on the previous 12-month total.

The high recall rate remains a key contributor to the prison capacity crisis, and was among the pressures that helped prompt early release schemes earlier this month.

The MoJ figures also show that 79,274 inmates were freed early from prison between September 2024 and June 2026 under the emergency measures the government brought in to tackle the overcrowding crisis.

The scheme, known as SDS40, cut the proportion of their sentence that some prisoners must serve in England and Wales from 50 per cent to 40 per cent; the MoJ said it was one of several policy changes likely to have contributed to the rise in recalls.

The MoJ said it was “vital those who break the rules can be hauled back to prison”, and pointed to policy changes that mean most offenders are now taken back into custody for 56 days before being released again – a fixed-term recall – rather than being held until the end of their sentence, as a likely factor behind the rise in recalls amid SDS40 releases.

The Howard League for Penal Reform called on the government to find a “lasting solution” to the overcrowding crisis, saying the “alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse”.

Rob Preece, the head of communications at the Howard League, said: “The prison system is under enormous pressure, with chronic overcrowding, staff shortages and awful conditions that make it close to impossible to rehabilitate people effectively. Imposing ever longer sentences has led us to this crisis, but the alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse.”

Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said the number of recalls must be addressed urgently to stop prison spaces being filled up again by people sent back to jail.

“A significant proportion of those released immediately go back to chaotic lives involving addiction, mental health problems and homelessness. Without adequate support and stable accommodation in place as soon as they step outside the gate, it is very difficult to break the revolving cycle of going back into prison too many are caught up in,” he said.

Pressure on the prison system has also coincided with continued high levels of self-harm and violence: safety in custody statistics showed 360 people in prison died in the 12 months to the end of September 2026, including 66 people who died in circumstances recorded as “self-inflicted”.

Self-harm incidents fell by 12 per cent in men’s prisons and by 3.8 per cent in women’s, even as prisons recorded 68,231 incidents in total in the 12 months to the end of June 2026 – a rate of one every eight minutes.

A separate dataset showed the number of serious offenders on probation charged with a serious further offence had increased for the third successive year, to a record number.

Of the 281 serious offenders charged, 119 were registered sexual offenders, 128 were murderers and four were terrorists or posed a terror risk, according to figures on multi-agency public protection arrangements.
output.standfirst: A permanent scheme under the Sentencing Act 2026 has replaced the emergency early-release measures, as new figures show recalls outnumbered releases in the first half of the year, up 27 per cent.

output.headline: Visit Norway responds to Trump with pride in its best toilets
output.bodyHtml:
Being dismissed by Donald Trump as a “shithouse country” might floor some nations. Not Norway’s tourist board, which responded by lifting the lid on some of the country’s loveliest lavatories.

“Are these the world’s best shit houses?” Visit Norway asked on its website, days after the US president vented his fury once more over failing to win the Nobel peace prize by describing Norway as a “shithouse country” at a rally on Sunday.

“Norway makes shit houses great again!” the agency declared above pictures of some of the country’s most striking public conveniences, adding: “These toilets are worth a visit, both when you really have to go – and when you don’t.”

Trump made the remark at a rally in Michigan days before the US midterm elections. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually,” he declared, using a term he has previously applied to Haiti, Libya, Somalia and Yemen.

He added that he would welcome migrants from some countries but not Norway, “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize”. Earlier this month, Trump denounced the decision to award the prize to Navi Pillay, a former international criminal court judge.

“This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” he said. “I never heard of this person. The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited … And we will not forget, Norway.”

Along 18 designated scenic routes around Norway, Visit Norway said, leading architects have been tasked with turning the humble wayside privy into an attraction in its own right; several have since won international architecture awards.

The agency showcased a series of designer public conveniences, many of them architecturally striking and all offering breathtaking vistas overlooking fjords, beside rushing rivers and foaming waterfalls, and at stunning scenic viewpoints.

They “invite you to take your time and enjoy the scenery, even if you don’t have any business to take care of”, Visit Norway said, highlighting – among others – the restrooms at the Stegastein viewpoint in the Sognefjord region of western Norway.

That comfort station, the tourist board noted with evident pride, has been ranked among the 10 best public toilets in the world by DesignCurial, the online architecture, design and interiors magazine.

Combining clean, minimalist lines with the fjord’s rugged and brooding landscape, the loos are known for their large, black-tinted glass windows, which give visitors a sweeping view from the throne while remaining invisible from the outside.

Also highlighted was the unique, wave-shaped Ureddplassen loo on the wild coast of Helgeland, the southernmost district of northern Norway, hailed by several international publications as the most scenic restroom in the world.

Among the others featured are the solar-powered modernist bog at the Utsikten viewpoint, the “Instagram-worthy” Tungeneset loo (“looks pretty good underneath the northern lights”), and the world-famous triangular “golden toilet” on Senja island.

Jens Kjeldsen, a rhetoric professor at the University of Bergen, said Visit Norway’s response was well judged under the circumstances. “It’s like the bully in kindergarten,” he told NRK public television. “If you get too serious, the bully wins.”

Evgenia Egorova, a senior consultant at Visit Norway, told the broadcaster that the response to its social media fightback had been immense. “The world needs a little laugh,” she said. “We thought: let’s meet them with kindness, and a little humour.”

Visit Norway said it had more stylish loos in the pipeline, including a forest-inspired latrine using dried wood from more than 60 trees. “Get ready for the pit stop of your life,” it urged, before signing off with a cheery: “Toodeloo!”

The Nobel peace prize is famously not awarded by the nation or even the government of Norway, but by the Nobel prize committee, which operates independently – something Trump “knows very well”, the foreign minister, Espen Barth Eide, said. “We have reminded him of that, in case anyone is wondering.”
output.standfirst: Visit Norway hit back at Donald Trump with droll pictures of the country’s prize-winning public toilets, days after the US president called Norway a ‘shithouse country’ for denying him the Nobel peace prize.
output.progress: Visit Norway is using humour and striking images of its toilets to turn Trump’s insult into a tourism moment.
